1219.title: The wedding feast
1219.hook: a meal to celebrate, even with one sheep (Bukhari)
1219.howItsDone: After a nikah, a Muslim family may hold a walimah, a wedding meal for relatives, friends and neighbors, which may be a simple dinner at home or a large hall reception; guests who are invited are encouraged to attend.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mahr, the bride's own free gift. Your line: hers alone.

Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf walks into Medina with a trace of yellow on his clothes, the color of a perfume, and the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ notices. What's this? I've married a woman of the Ansar, he says. The Prophet asks what he gave her. A date stone's weight of gold. Then the Prophet tells him the next thing to do. Not buy a house. Not throw a party to impress the town. In Sahih al-Bukhari, his words come down to this: hold a wedding meal, even if it's only one sheep. The marriage is made. Now feed people. Today's word: walimah.
screen: `A TRACE OF YELLOW ON HIS CLOTHES.` → `I'VE MARRIED.` → `HOLD A MEAL, EVEN WITH ONE SHEEP.`

segments.voice: Walimah is the wedding feast, the meal that celebrates and announces a marriage. The nikah needed a public celebration; this is it, served on plates. First, the size. Even one sheep. The point isn't the menu. It's that there should be a meal at all, shared, so the marriage is known and the joy is passed around. Second, what a feast can look like. In Bukhari, the companion Anas describes a wedding meal the Prophet gave with no bread and no meat at all: dates, dried yogurt and butter, spread on a leather mat. Third, who's at the table. A report in Bukhari, from Abu Hurayrah, is blunt: the worst food is the food of a wedding feast where the rich are invited and the poor are left out. The walimah can be humble. What it can't be, in that report, is a party that shuts the door on the poor. Fourth, the guests' side. Bukhari also keeps the instruction that when someone is invited to a wedding feast, they should come. Showing up is part of it. The schools discuss how strong these are: whether holding a walimah is required or strongly recommended, and when a guest may excuse himself. A marriage is made with words. Then it's celebrated with food, and the guest list reaches past the people who can invite you back. The feast tells the town these two are married, and it turns a private joy into something a neighbor can taste.
screen: `EVEN ONE SHEEP.` · `DATES AND BUTTER ON A LEATHER MAT.` · `THE WORST FOOD: RICH IN, POOR OUT.` · `WHEN YOU'RE INVITED, COME.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the best meal you ever shared, not the most expensive, the best: who was at the table, and what was on it? Notice how much of the memory is the food and how much is the people. Then picture a simple table for one small good thing that hasn't been celebrated, and one person you'd invite who's rarely invited; if you pray, you can give thanks in your own words.
Walimah. The wedding feast, held to celebrate and announce a marriage, even if it's only one sheep, with the poor at the table too. Today's word.
Your line: feed people. Even one sheep, even dates on a leather mat, with the poor invited. Until tomorrow.

1220.title: Rights in marriage
1220.hook: kindness, provision, consultation, and dignity on both sides
1220.howItsDone: Muslim teaching on marriage sets out rights for both spouses, including kind treatment, financial provision by the husband, and mutual consultation; imams may return to these verses and to the hadith about being best to one's family in marriage sermons and counseling.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the walimah, with the poor at the table. Your line: feed people.

Someone once asked Aisha a very domestic question. What did the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ do at home? Not in the mosque. Not leading people. At home. Her answer, kept in Sahih al-Bukhari, is short. He used to be in the service of his family, she said, and when the time for prayer came, he went out to pray. Now the feast is over, the guests have gone home, and two people are left with each other and a long list of ordinary days. What do they owe each other? Today: rights in marriage.
screen: `WHAT DID HE DO AT HOME?` → `IN THE SERVICE OF HIS FAMILY.` → `WHAT DO THEY OWE EACH OTHER?`

segments.voice: Surah two, verse two hundred twenty-eight, in Pickthall's translation: "And they (women) have rights similar to those (of men) over them in kindness." Rights running both ways. The same verse goes on to say that men have a degree above them, and commentators explain that degree in different ways. One early reading, attributed to Ibn Abbas, says the degree is that a husband gives up some of what's due to him. Next, a picture of closeness. Surah two again, about husband and wife: "They are raiment for you and ye are raiment for them." Clothing. Each covers the other, keeps the other warm, sits closest to the skin. Then, the practical rights. Provision: the Qur'an tells a husband to spend on his household from what he has, the wealthy from his wealth, the one with little from what he's been given. Consultation: in surah two, even when to wean a baby is to be settled by both parents, by mutual consent and consulting each other. Kindness: surah four tells husbands to live with their wives in kindness, even when there's something about them they dislike, because there may be much good in it. Last, dignity. In a report in the collection of at-Tirmidhi, the Prophet says the best of you is the best to his family, and adds: I am the best of you to my family. That's the measure: not how someone behaves in public, but how they are in the kitchen. The schools spell out these rights in detail, and differ on some. But the frame is the one from the nikah: a contract of mercy, with rights written on both sides.

segments.voice: Picture the place you live, the kitchen, the sink, the pile by the door, and the people you share it with, or call most. Ask what each of them quietly carries, and choose one thing you could take off their hands without being asked or announcing it. If you pray, you can ask in your own words to be good to your family.
Rights in marriage. Kindness, provision, consultation and dignity, owed on both sides: each spouse is raiment for the other. Today's word.
Your line: rights both ways. Each one raiment for the other. That's today, done.

1221.title: Divorce, permitted not loved
1221.hook: permitted but disliked, with waiting periods and kindness
1221.howItsDone: Muslim couples in difficulty are encouraged to seek reconciliation, for example through family members or an imam, before divorce; a divorce is followed by a waiting period during which the couple may reconcile, and a wife may seek a release of her own, called khul'.

segments.voice: Yesterday, rights in marriage, owed both ways. Your line: rights both ways.

A woman comes to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ about her husband, Thabit ibn Qays, and she starts by defending him. I don't fault him, she says, not his character and not his faith. But she can't stay. She's afraid that if she stays, she'll fall short of what she owes in the marriage. The Prophet doesn't lecture her. He asks one practical question: will you give him back his garden? The garden was his gift to her. Yes, she says. So he tells Thabit to take the garden back and let her go. In Sahih al-Bukhari, a marriage ends without a villain. Today's word: talaq.
screen: `I DON'T FAULT HIM.` → `WILL YOU GIVE BACK HIS GARDEN?` → `A MARRIAGE ENDS WITHOUT A VILLAIN.`

segments.voice: Talaq is divorce, and in Islamic law the husband's release of the marriage. A hadith in the Sunan of Abu Dawud says that of the things Allah has permitted, the one He dislikes most is divorce. Hadith scholars have debated its chain. Some readers hear the same in the verses themselves: a door that exists, not meant to be swung lightly. Next, what comes before it. Surah four says that when a breach is feared between husband and wife, an arbiter is to be appointed from his family and an arbiter from hers, and if they want to set things right, Allah will bring them together. Talk first, with people who love both sides. Then, how the door is built. Surah two, in Pickthall's translation: "Divorce must be pronounced twice and then (a woman) must be retained in honour or released in kindness." Each of those first two times, there is a waiting period, and during it the couple can come back together. Room to cool off, and at the end, either way, kindness. The same verse forbids taking back what was given to her, with one exception, the story from the hook: when the wife asks to leave and returns the gift, it has its own name, khul'. She can seek her release too. The schools differ on details, including what happens when someone says the word three times at once. Permitted, because sometimes a marriage can't go on. Not loved, because it's still a breaking. And even the breaking has manners.
screen: `PERMITTED, BUT DISLIKED.` · `AN ARBITER FROM EACH FAMILY.` · `TWICE, WITH TIME TO RETURN.` · `SHE CAN SEEK HER RELEASE, TOO.` · then, large: `RELEASED IN KINDNESS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something that has ended for you, or needs to, and ask: could I leave it without making the other side a villain, with a thank-you, an apology, an honest goodbye? Let one kind sentence form; if you pray, you can ask for gentleness in endings.
Talaq. Divorce in Islam: permitted but disliked, with arbiters first, waiting periods, a way back, and parting in kindness. Today's word.
Your line: permitted, not loved. Even an ending can be kind. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1222.title: Children's rights
1222.hook: a good name, education, fairness between them
1222.howItsDone: Islamic law counts choosing a good name and teaching a child to read, pray and earn a living among a parent's duties; scholars teach that gifts between children should be fair, following the story of Nu'man ibn Bashir.

segments.voice: Yesterday, talaq, and your line: permitted, not loved. A door the law leaves open, with waiting and kindness built around it.

The boy in this story is the one who told it. Nu'man ibn Bashir remembered his father walking him to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. His father had given him a gift and wanted the Prophet to witness it. The Prophet asked one question: had he given the same to each of his children? No. And the Prophet would not witness it. Nu'man remembered his father taking the gift back. Today: what children are owed in Islamic law, and why fairness sits at the center.
screen: `A FATHER WANTS A WITNESS.` → `ONE QUESTION: THE SAME FOR EACH?` → `THE GIFT GOES BACK.`

segments.voice: Day two hundred seventy-one showed the Prophet's tenderness with children. Today is the law's side. The fiqh books talk about a child's rights the way they talk about a spouse's: things owed, not favors. Three of them. First, a good name. Reports in Sahih Muslim tell of the Prophet changing harsh or heavy names into gentler ones. A name is said across a whole life, by teachers and friends and, one day, on a grave, so choosing it well counts among a parent's duties. Second, education. A report in Ibn Majah calls seeking knowledge a duty on every Muslim, and jurists teach that a parent owes a child the teaching that makes it possible: how to read, how to pray, how to live with people, and a way to earn a living. Third, fairness, and here is Nu'man's story again. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet tells his father to fear God and be just between his children. Not identical in every detail, since children need different things, but no child made to feel like the favorite's shadow. The jurists argue over the edges: some hold that gifts to sons and daughters should be exactly equal; others follow the shares of inheritance. Both start from the same story, where favoritism is a wrong, not a private taste. And underneath all three, the Qur'an forbids killing children out of fear of poverty, and promises that God provides for them and for their parents. Before a name or a lesson comes life itself.
screen: `RIGHTS OWED, NOT FAVORS.` · `FIRST, A GOOD NAME.` · `THEN, AN EDUCATION.` · `FAIRNESS: FEAR GOD, BE JUST.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the children in your life: your own, nieces and nephews, students, the kids on your street. Picture them in a row. Notice if one face comes easier than the others, the funny one, the one who looks like you; no guilt, just notice. Then go down the row slowly and give each one a moment of real attention, their name and one thing they need that is theirs alone, and if you pray, hold each name in turn.
Children's rights. In Islamic law, what a child is owed: life, a good name, an education, and fairness between them and their brothers and sisters. Today's word.
Your line: fair to each. No child left in the favorite's shadow. Until tomorrow.

1223.title: Inheritance in practice
1223.hook: fixed shares for family, and up to a third by will
1223.howItsDone: When a Muslim dies, debts are paid first, then any will of up to a third is carried out, and the rest is divided among family members by the shares set out in surah four, often with a scholar's help.

segments.voice: Yesterday, children's rights, and your line: fair to each. A father walked his son to the Prophet, and the gift went back.

Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas lies sick in Mecca, sure he is about to die. He has some wealth and one daughter to inherit from him. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ comes to visit, and Sa'd asks straight out: may I give all my wealth away in charity? It sounds like a beautiful question. The Prophet says no. Then half? No. Then a third? A third, the Prophet answers, and a third is a lot. Tradition says Sa'd recovered. But that bedside bargain became a line in Islamic law.
screen: `SA'D ON HIS SICKBED.` → `ALL? NO. HALF? NO.` → `A THIRD, AND A THIRD IS A LOT.`

segments.voice: Islamic inheritance works in two layers. The first is fixed by the Qur'an. In surah four, God names the shares: what children receive, what parents receive, what a husband or wife receives. The verses call them an ordinance from God, and the jurists built a whole science around them, called fara'id, the obligatory shares. You don't choose these. The second layer is yours. Before the shares are divided, the debts are paid and the will is carried out, and the will can reach up to a third of what is left. That third is where a person can remember a friend, a cause, a mosque, a stranger who was kind. One limit: a report in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi says there is no bequest to an heir. Those who already have a share from the Qur'an can't be given extra by will; the third is for people the shares don't reach. And the Prophet gave Sa'd a reason. In Sahih al-Bukhari, he says leaving your heirs well off is better than leaving them dependent, holding out their hands to people. So the limit isn't a limit on generosity. It points generosity two ways at once: to family, through the shares, and to the wider world, through the third. A family may sit with a scholar to work out the exact shares, and the schools disagree on some rarer cases. But the shape holds: the debts, the third, then the shares.
screen: `LAYER ONE: SHARES FIXED IN SURAH FOUR.` · `LAYER TWO: A WILL, UP TO A THIRD.` · `NO BEQUEST TO AN HEIR.` · `LEAVE THEM WELL OFF, NOT DEPENDENT.`

segments.voice: Write a very simple will, only in your head for now: start with what you owe, anyone you'd want paid back, any promise you'd want kept. Then think about your third, not the money but the people outside your family: a teacher, a neighbor, a place that fed you once. Hold one name, and if it feels right, you can write it down later.
Inheritance in practice. Fixed shares for the family from the Qur'an, and up to a third by will for those the shares don't reach. Today's word.
Your line: a third by will. Family through the shares, the wider world through the third. See you tomorrow.

1224.title: Trade and honesty
1224.hook: the honest merchant is with the prophets (Tirmidhi)
1224.howItsDone: Muslim merchants are taught to disclose defects, give full measure and avoid false oaths in selling, and Islamic law gives buyers a right to return goods with a hidden defect.

segments.voice: Yesterday, inheritance in practice, and your line: a third by will. The family's shares are fixed; the third reaches the ones they don't.

A market in Medina. Grain is heaped up for sale, dry and golden on top. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is walking past, and he pushes his hand down into the pile. His fingers come out wet. The seller says the rain got to it. Then why not put the wet part on top, the Prophet asks, so people can see it? And he says: whoever cheats is not of me. Today: trade, and the one thing a market can't run without.
screen: `A HEAP OF GRAIN IN MEDINA.` → `A HAND PUSHED INSIDE.` → `WET UNDERNEATH.`

segments.voice: In these texts the market isn't a dirty place. Tradition says the Prophet himself worked in trade before his mission, and the Qur'an mentions the caravans of winter and summer without embarrassment. What it watches is the scale. Surah eighty-three opens, in Pickthall's words, "Woe unto the defrauders," people who demand full measure when they buy and give short measure when they sell. Then the reward. In a report in Tirmidhi, the Prophet says the truthful, trustworthy merchant will be with the prophets, the truthful and the martyrs. Someone who sells phone cases, or tomatoes, or used cars, in that company, for telling the truth about the goods. A report in Sahih al-Bukhari makes it practical. Buyer and seller keep the right to back out until they part. If both speak truly and make things clear, their sale is blessed; if they hide things and lie, its blessing is wiped out. Two verbs: speak truly, and make clear. Not lying is half. The other half is the grain story: showing the flaw before the buyer finds it. That's why the fiqh books give buyers a right to return goods with a hidden defect the seller didn't mention. Honesty isn't left to the seller's mood; the law builds it into the contract. The honest merchant isn't a saint who wandered into a market. It's someone who puts the wet grain on top.

1225.hook: interest is forbidden (2:275), and the reasons scholars give
1225.howItsDone: Muslims who keep this rule avoid paying or receiving interest, using Islamic banks, interest-free loans within families and communities, or other arrangements; scholars and fiqh councils still discuss how the rule applies to modern banking.

segments.voice: Yesterday, trade and honesty: a sale is blessed when both sides speak truly and make things clear. Your line: the honest merchant.

Yesterday the market was praised. Today the Qur'an draws a hard line through it. In surah two, it describes people who say trade is just like riba, just like charging interest. Both are deals, both make money; what's the difference? The verse answers without arguing, in Pickthall's words: "Allah permitteth trading and forbiddeth usury." Two things that look alike on a spreadsheet, one allowed and one forbidden. The passage calls believers to give up what remains owed to them of riba, and warns those who won't.
screen: `TRADE IS JUST LIKE RIBA, THEY SAY.` → `PERMITTED, AND FORBIDDEN.` → `GIVE UP WHAT REMAINS.`

segments.voice: Pickthall renders riba as usury; it's also called interest: an extra amount charged on a loan just because time has passed. The Qur'an ties it to growth. In surah thirty, what you give in riba so that it may grow on other people's wealth does not grow with God, while what you give in charity does. Two kinds of increase, pointed opposite ways. The hadith sharpen the line. In Sahih Muslim, Jabir reports that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ cursed the one who consumes riba, the one who pays it, the one who writes it down and the two witnesses, and said they are all alike. The whole transaction, not only the lender. Why? The Qur'an gives one reason in the same passage: if you repent, you keep your capital, and you neither wrong nor are wronged. Scholars built on that. Some point to need: the borrower is often the one in trouble, and interest lets the strong profit from the weak one's bad season. Some point to risk: in trade both sides can win or lose, but a fixed interest payment lets the lender gain whatever happens to the borrower. Some point to the community: the Qur'an elsewhere warns against wealth circulating only among the rich. And how this meets today's banks is still argued. Some fiqh councils have ruled that ordinary bank interest is riba; some individual scholars have argued otherwise. That conversation leads straight into tomorrow.
